name: Ivan Yilmaz

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We aren't tied to any company, union, party or government. Everything you say stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. Is that all right?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Fine. I'm not much of a talker, but go on. If it's about computers, I should tell you now that my kids set up my phone.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I run a 250-tonne stamping press at a metal works that makes brackets and back panels for washing machines. Steel coil goes in one end, the press comes down, and out come the shapes. I check the die, that's the steel mould that cuts the shape, I watch for burrs and splits, and I swap the coil when it runs out. Six to two, five days, overtime on Saturdays when the orders are up. I like that it's simple and you can see what you made by lunchtime. The noise gets you, though, even with the ear defenders, and my back's not what it was.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: How long have you been on that press?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Fourteen years on that press, eighteen at the company. The foreman, Rudi, trained me. He retired last spring and I still catch myself looking for him.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say what I always say, which is that the newspapers get excited about everything. Last year it was hydrogen, before that it was something else. I wouldn't post anything, I don't post.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I'd be glad. I've never used any of these AI things and I don't plan to. My press doesn't care what the internet thinks, it just wants the coil fed straight.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Nothing. Keep doing my shifts, keep the Saturday overtime when it's there, keep putting a bit away each month. We've got about a year's worth of money saved, and Elif's salon does well, so I'm not losing sleep.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Same as now.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there any part of the plant where you think even the small changes would show up?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Maybe the office side. The planners, the people who do the orders. They'd get the AI first. On the floor we'd just carry on with the same presses.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Does your company already use any of these tools?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The bosses spent a lot on a new computer system two years ago and we still use the paper sheets. So no, I don't think much would change.

S0.say: Newspapers get excited about everything, last year hydrogen and before that something else. I wouldn't post anything, because I don't post.
S0.think: I'd be glad, because I've never used these AI things and don't plan to. The press just needs the coil fed straight, whatever the internet thinks.
S0.do: Keeps doing his shifts and Saturday overtime and keeps putting a bit away each month. Relies on about a year's savings and his wife's salon.
S0.quote: My press doesn't care what the internet thinks, it just wants the coil fed straight.
S0.fieldNote: Ivan is brief and dry, and very sure of himself in a quiet future. His calm is backed by a year's savings and his wife's business. He expects any small change to land in the office, not on the press floor.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second one is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many tasks in many jobs. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. But most people still have work, and society has time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say change happens, it always has. Some of it'll be good, some won't. People should keep their heads.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Between us, I'd be worried about the presses getting automatic feeding and cameras. That's been talked about for years, and if it gets cheaper, they'll do it. Then they'd need one man for three presses instead of one each, and I'm not the youngest or the quickest on a screen.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd wait and see what the company actually does. If they bring in the cameras, I'd learn what I have to, but I wouldn't go to evening classes on my own. I'd put more into savings, maybe 300 a month instead of 200, and I'd stop the plan to change the car this year.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy. It's in the back of my head.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you go on a course if the company didn't make you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Probably not, if I'm honest. I'd learn the new screen if they put it in front of me, but I wouldn't go looking for it. That's just how I am.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you do if they did cut jobs?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: There are other metal works around here, four or five within twenty minutes. If my place went funny, I'd go to one of them. They all still need someone on the presses.

S1.say: Change happens, it always has, and some of it's good and some isn't. People should keep their heads.
S1.think: I worry the presses would get automatic feeding and cameras, so they'd need one man for three presses. I'm not the youngest or quickest on a screen.
S1.do: Waits to see what the company actually does and learns only what's required. Raises monthly savings from 200 to 300 and puts off changing the car this year.
S1.feel: Uneasy, with the worry sitting at the back of his head.
S1.quote: I'd learn the new screen if they put it in front of me, but I wouldn't go looking for it.
S1.fieldNote: Ivan's public line is calm common sense, but privately he knows exactly how his job would shrink. He refuses to retrain unless it's put in front of him. His fallback is the four or five similar metal works nearby, a real advantage he relies on.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. With robots it reaches hands-on work too. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say the government had better sort this out, because it's going to be a mess. I don't take sides much, but this would be one where you'd need everyone pulling the same way.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I'd think the press job's gone. If a robot can do anything, it can feed a coil and spot a split. And the other metal works would go the same way at the same time, so there'd be nowhere to go.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: First, I'd go through the money with Elif, line by line. I'd stop the overtime spending, cancel the holiday, and keep the car till it dies. I'd keep going to work until they let me go. And I'd ask my brother about his garage, he does tyres and brakes, maybe I could help there for a while.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed. I'd be up at night, I think, which I never am.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Two years' warning. Does that give you any room to do something about it?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No, that's what bothers me. Two years is nothing. I'm not going to become a programmer in two years, and it wouldn't help anyway. In two years all I can do is count the money twice.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would Elif's salon be a safety net?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Probably, yes, for a while. People would still want their hair cut by a person, I'd think. But if everyone's out of work, they cut their own hair. Elif says that already happened during the lockdown.

S2.say: The government had better sort this out, because it's going to be a mess. I don't take sides much, but this needs everyone pulling the same way.
S2.think: I think the press job's gone, because a robot could feed a coil and spot a split. The other metal works would go at the same time, so there'd be nowhere to go.
S2.do: Goes through the household money line by line with his wife, cancels the holiday and keeps the old car. Works until let go and asks his brother about helping at his tyre and brake garage.
S2.feel: Alarmed and losing sleep, which he never does.
S2.quote: In two years all I can do is count the money twice.
S2.fieldNote: The fast scenario removes Ivan's main comfort, the nearby metal works, because they'd all change at once. He goes straight to budgets and family rather than training. His wife's lockdown experience makes him doubt the salon would carry them.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say there's time, so let's be sensible. Governments, companies, everyone should get a plan together. No point panicking.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd still be slow to move, I know that. But five years means the mortgage would be a lot smaller, and Deniz would be nearly done with school. I'd think about how to get to 2031 with the least damage.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd overpay the mortgage, maybe 15,000 in the first year out of savings. I'd stay on the press as long as it's there. And maybe, in the second or third year, I'd ask the company about moving onto the die repair side, because that's still hands-on and I know the dies already.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but I could breathe a bit.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why die repair?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Rudi used to say a die tells you when it's tired, if you listen. I've listened to dies for fourteen years, I just never thought a robot would learn to listen too. So die repair would buy me a bit, not forever.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you wouldn't go to classes on your own. Would five years change that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: To be honest, maybe I'd do the course if the company paid and it was in work time. On my own, at night, I'd keep putting it off.

S3.say: There's time, so let's be sensible and have governments and companies get a plan together. There's no point panicking.
S3.think: I'd still be slow to move, but in five years the mortgage would be much smaller and Deniz nearly done with school. I'd think about getting to 2031 with the least damage.
S3.do: Overpays the mortgage by about 15,000 from savings in the first year and stays on the press as long as it lasts. In the second or third year, asks to move to die repair, taking a course only if it's paid and in work time.
S3.feel: Anxious, but able to breathe a bit.
S3.quote: I've listened to dies for fourteen years, I just never thought a robot would learn to listen too.
S3.fieldNote: With five years Ivan's thinking turns to damage limitation: paying down the house and moving one step sideways into die repair. He's honest that he'd only train if it's paid and in work hours. His memory of his old foreman Rudi gives his trade knowledge a human face.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last one is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is a long time. A lot can happen. Maybe it comes, maybe it doesn't, so let's not lose our heads.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Between us, ten years means I'd be fifty-three with the house almost paid and the kids grown or nearly. If I get there with the job, I'd be all right. That's how I'd look at it, just get to the finish line.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd do nothing big at first, keep working, keep saving. After a few years, if it looked real, I'd pay off the rest of the mortgage and maybe move to die repair. I'd talk to Deniz about not going into the press work, because I wouldn't want him starting where I'm finishing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, like a cloud a long way off.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell Deniz to do instead?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Something with people. A nurse, maybe, or something with his hands where you have to talk to someone. I'd tell him a robot can bend steel, but it can't calm down an old lady. I don't know if that's even true by then.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there anything you'd start now, with ten years to go?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: You know, I'd probably do the same as with five years, just later. That's the honest answer. I'm not one for early.

S4.say: Ten years is a long time and a lot can happen, so maybe it comes and maybe it doesn't. Let's not lose our heads.
S4.think: I'd be fifty-three with the house almost paid and the kids grown or nearly. If I get there with the job, I'd be all right, so it's about getting to the finish line.
S4.do: Keeps working and saving without any big move at first. Pays off the mortgage and maybe moves to die repair if it looks real after a few years, and steers his son away from press work.
S4.feel: Uneasy, like a cloud a long way off.
S4.quote: I'd tell him a robot can bend steel, but it can't calm down an old lady.
S4.fieldNote: Ten years lets Ivan treat AGI as a finish line he might reach before it hits him. His plan is the same as with five years, only later, and he admits he's 'not one for early'. His advice to his son is the clearest change in his family plans.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one, easily. What would help is honest notice from the company, so we know when, and a bit of money to tide us over. And somebody to tell me straight what jobs are left, not a leaflet.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Not really. Maybe that people like me aren't against things, we just like to see them work first. I'm not scared of robots, I'm scared of being fifty with no trade.

headlineQuote: I'm not scared of robots, I'm scared of being fifty with no trade.
portrait: Ivan Yilmaz is 43, has run a stamping press at a metal works for fourteen years, and is married to Elif, who owns a hair salon, with two children. He's dry, practical and slow to change, never uses AI and only trains when it's put in front of him. A year of savings, his wife's business and plenty of similar factories nearby keep him calm or uneasy in the milder pictures. When AGI comes in two years and every plant changes at once, he becomes alarmed and turns to budgets and his brother's garage, while more time lets him pay down the house and edge into die repair.
biggestWorry: AGI by 2028 worries him most, because two years is nothing and every metal works around him would change at the same time.
whatWouldHelp: Honest notice from the company, some money to tide them over, and someone telling him straight what jobs are left.
